options.label: A
options.text: Purchasing power is about 20.0% higher than planned

options.label: B
options.text: Purchasing power is about 4.0% lower than planned

options.label: C
options.text: Purchasing power is about 17.5% lower than planned

options.label: D
options.text: Purchasing power is exactly the same as planned

options.label: E
options.text: Purchasing power is about 17.5% higher than planned

explanation: After five years, expected prices are multiplied by 1.02⁵ and actual prices by 1.06⁵. The actual pension’s purchasing power relative to the planned purchasing power is (1.02 ÷ 1.06)⁵ ≈ 0.825, about 17.5% lower. In initial-year dollars, the planned monthly pension is about $2,717 and the actual pension about $2,242.

prompt: Country X has zero unexpected inflation — actual inflation always equals expected inflation. Country Y has highly volatile and unpredictable inflation. Which of the following correctly compares the wealth redistribution between lenders and borrowers in the two countries?

options.label: A
options.text: Predictable inflation creates larger arbitrary transfers than unexpected inflation

options.label: B
options.text: Only predictable inflation changes the general price level

options.label: C
options.text: Only unexpected inflation allows contracts to adjust before signing

options.label: D
options.text: Unexpected inflation creates less predictable real repayments than anticipated inflation

options.label: E
options.text: Both inflation patterns preserve every fixed contract’s real value

explanation: is about the UNEXPECTED component of inflation. If actual inflation always equals expected inflation (Country X), nominal contracts are correctly calibrated and no arbitrary redistribution occurs - lenders earn their planned real return and borrowers pay their planned real cost; country Y's volatile, unpredictable inflation generates continuous, arbitrary wealth transfers depending on the direction and magnitude of each surprise.

prompt: A union negotiated a 3-year fixed nominal wage contract for its workers expecting 2% annual inflation. Actual inflation during those 3 years was 5%, 5%, and 4%. Which of the following best describes the outcome for the workers and the employer?

options.label: A
options.text: Workers lose purchasing power; employers pay lower real wages than expected

options.label: B
options.text: The employer lost because unexpected inflation forces companies to rehire workers at higher rates

options.label: C
options.text: Both workers and employer were equally affected by the unexpected inflation

options.label: D
options.text: Workers gained because nominal wages are always better than real wages

options.label: E
options.text: Workers gain; employer loses — because nominal wages rose each year

explanation: This applies the unexpected-inflation redistribution to wage contracts; workers agreed to nominal wages based on 2% expected inflation - they are analogous to lenders; the employer pays fixed nominal wages - analogous to a borrower. With actual inflation of 5%, 5%, 4% vs. expected 2%, 2%, 2%, real wages are lower than planned (by approximately 3, 3, and 2 pp per year); workers lose; employer gains - a wealth transfer from workers to the employer driven by unexpected inflation.

prompt: A person saved $50,000 in a fixed-rate CD (certificate of deposit) at 3% nominal annual interest, expecting 2% inflation. If actual inflation is 5%, what is the approximate real gain or loss on this saving after one year?

options.label: A
options.text: Real gain of $1,500 (the 3% nominal return)

options.label: B
options.text: Approximately −2% real return, or a $1,000 purchasing-power loss

options.label: C
options.text: Real gain of $500 (3% − 2% = 1% expected real return, × $50,000)

options.label: D
options.text: Real gain of $2,500 — inflation increases the value of savings

options.label: E
options.text: Breakeven — the 3% nominal return always exactly offsets inflation

explanation: Planned real return = 3% - 2% = 1% = $500; actual real return = 3% - 5% = -2% = -$1,000. The unexpected 3 pp of extra inflation (5% vs. 2%) wiped out the planned $500 gain and produced a $1,000 real loss; the bank (borrower of the depositor's funds) benefits from this outcome - it pays back deposits in cheaper dollars; the saver-as-lender loses; the bank-as-borrower gains; classic MEA-1.H.1.

prompt: A corporation issued 10-year bonds at a fixed 5% nominal coupon when inflation was expected to remain at 3%. Actual inflation over the 10-year period averages 7%. Which of the following best describes the impact on bondholders and the corporation?

options.label: A
options.text: Both parties preserve the real repayment they originally expected

options.label: B
options.text: The lender gains purchasing power; the borrower gains purchasing power

options.label: C
options.text: The lender loses purchasing power; the borrower gains purchasing power

options.label: D
options.text: The lender gains purchasing power; the borrower loses purchasing power

options.label: E
options.text: Both parties gain purchasing power relative to their expectations

explanation: Bondholders (lenders) planned for a +2% real return (5% nominal - 3% expected inflation); actual real return = 5% - 7% = -2%; they lose 4 pp of real return compared to expectations. The corporation (borrower) planned to pay a +2% real borrowing cost; actual real borrowing cost = -2%; the corporation gains 4 pp - it borrowed at what turns out to be a negative real interest rate; this is a large wealth transfer from bondholder to corporation caused entirely by unexpected inflation.

prompt: Economists sometimes say unexpected inflation acts as "an arbitrary tax on creditors and a subsidy to debtors." Explain what this means.

options.label: A
options.text: This phrase only applies during hyperinflation, not moderate unexpected inflation

options.label: B
options.text: A metaphor for creditors' losses and debtors' gains, without an actual tax

options.label: C
options.text: Inflation literally taxes lenders and gives cash payments to borrowers through the tax code

options.label: D
options.text: Unexpected inflation creates a literal tax that the government collects from lenders and redistributes to borrowers

options.label: E
options.text: Inflation only taxes debtors and subsidizes creditors

explanation: The "tax on creditors / subsidy to debtors" metaphor captures the redistribution precisely; creditors lose real value involuntarily - like a tax; debtors gain real value involuntarily - like a subsidy. No government action is required; the mechanism operates through the erosion of fixed nominal claims; the analogy highlights that the transfer is one-sided: creditors do not consent to this "tax," and debtors did not earn this "subsidy." Both are consequences of an unexpected surprise in the price level.

prompt: A country unexpectedly experiences sustained deflation for three years. Which of the following correctly identifies the direction of wealth redistribution?

options.label: A
options.text: Deflation equally harms both lenders and borrowers

options.label: B
options.text: Borrowers lose and lenders gain as real debt burdens rise

options.label: C
options.text: Deflation redistributes wealth from lenders to borrowers, same as inflation

options.label: D
options.text: Deflation redistributes wealth from the government to private citizens

options.label: E
options.text: Deflation has no redistributive effects — only inflation redistributes wealth

explanation: covers both unexpected inflation AND unexpected deflation; deflation reverses the redistribution: lenders gain (receive higher real value) and borrowers lose (repay higher real value). This is why unexpected deflation can be economically damaging - heavily indebted borrowers (firms, households, governments) face higher real debt burdens, potentially triggering defaults, which can spiral into deeper economic contraction.

prompt: During the Great Depression of the 1930s, the United States experienced severe deflation. Which of the following best explains how this deflation redistributed wealth?

options.label: A
options.text: Deflation benefited both lenders and borrowers equally

options.label: B
options.text: Deflation helped borrowers because prices fell, making goods cheaper to buy

options.label: C
options.text: Deflation helped borrowers because the government forgave debts during deflation

options.label: D
options.text: Deflation was neutral — it reduced both debt and income proportionally

options.label: E
options.text: Real debts become harder to repay, increasing default risk

explanation: The Great Depression deflation is a classic example of unexpected deflation harming borrowers; farm prices fell dramatically, but farm mortgages remained at their nominal levels - farmers' real debt burden soared. Many defaulted; the real-value increase of nominal debts was the deflation analogue of inflation eroding nominal debt; applies symmetrically: unexpected deflation → wealth transferred from borrowers to lenders, potentially causing widespread debt distress.

prompt: Two mortgage borrowers took out identical $300,000 fixed-rate mortgages at 5% nominal interest. Borrower A's loan was issued in a year when inflation was expected and remained at 3%. Borrower B's loan was issued in a year when inflation was expected at 3% but unexpectedly rose to 7%. Which borrower was better off in real terms from unexpected inflation?

options.label: A
options.text: Both borrowers have identical real borrowing costs

options.label: B
options.text: Borrower A has a lower real borrowing cost than B

options.label: C
options.text: Borrower B has a lower real borrowing cost than A

options.label: D
options.text: Both borrowers have higher real costs than they expected

options.label: E
options.text: Borrower B has a higher real borrowing cost than expected

explanation: Borrower A: real mortgage cost = 5%-3% = 2% as planned - no surprise; borrower B: planned real cost = 5%-3% = 2%, actual real cost = 5%-7% = -2%. Borrower B got a 4 pp surprise reduction in real borrowing cost - the unexpected inflation made their debt cheaper in real terms; the lender (bank) suffered the corresponding 4 pp surprise loss; fixed-rate mortgage borrowers uniquely benefit when actual inflation exceeds the rate priced into their fixed nominal interest rate.

prompt: A landlord has 50 apartments, all with 2-year fixed-rent leases signed when inflation was expected to be 2%. Actual inflation turns out to be 6%. A neighboring landlord has leases that include a clause allowing rent increases equal to the actual CPI change each year. Which landlord is more harmed by the unexpected inflation, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Neither landlord is affected — rental income is always protected from inflation

options.label: B
options.text: The fixed-rent landlord; full CPI indexation protects the other landlord

options.label: C
options.text: The landlord with CPI-indexed leases is more harmed because the CPI-adjustment costs more administratively

options.label: D
options.text: The fixed-rent landlord benefits because tenants pay more in nominal terms each year

options.label: E
options.text: Both landlords are equally harmed because they own the same number of apartments

explanation: The fixed-rent landlord is harmed because: planned real rent income = nominal rent ÷ (1+2% per year); actual real rent = same nominal ÷ (1+6% per year). The 4 pp extra inflation erodes real rental income each year, transferring real value to tenants; the CPI-indexed landlord automatically adjusts rent to match actual CPI - no surprise occurs, no arbitrary redistribution; this illustrates how indexing contracts eliminates the unexpected-inflation redistribution problem.

prompt: Which of the following groups is most likely to favor unexpectedly high inflation, and which is most likely to oppose it? Explain.

options.label: A
options.text: Bondholders favor high inflation; cash holders oppose it

options.label: B
options.text: Lenders favor high inflation; borrowers oppose it

options.label: C
options.text: Workers favor high inflation; retirees favor it equally

options.label: D
options.text: Both groups are indifferent because redistribution balances out

options.label: E
options.text: Fixed-rate debtors tend to gain; fixed-nominal claim holders tend to lose

explanation: Borrowers hold fixed nominal liabilities - they gain when inflation erodes the real value of what they owe; lenders hold fixed nominal assets - they lose when inflation erodes the real value of what they are owed. This creates a structural conflict of interest: debtors prefer unexpected inflation; creditors prefer price stability or unexpected deflation; identifies this as the core social cost - arbitrary redistribution that creates winners and losers who did not choose these outcomes.

prompt: A company took out a $1 million fixed-rate bank loan at 6% nominal interest when expected inflation was 4% (expected real rate = 2%). Actual inflation over the loan period was 8%. Calculate the approximate real rate the company paid and determine whether it gained or lost relative to its expectations.

options.label: A
options.text: Approximately −2% real borrowing cost, 4 points below expectations

options.label: B
options.text: Real rate paid ≈ 6%; the company paid as contracted

options.label: C
options.text: Real rate paid ≈ 10%; inflation always adds to the nominal rate

options.label: D
options.text: Real rate paid ≈ 2%; the company paid exactly as expected, with no gain or loss

options.label: E
options.text: Real rate paid ≈ 6%; fixed nominal rates are always equal to the real rate

explanation: Expected real rate = 6% - 4% = +2%; actual real rate = 6% - 8% = -2%. The company (borrower) benefited by 4 percentage points - it planned to pay 2% real but actually received a -2% real rate (lender effectively paid the company to borrow); the bank (lender) planned to earn +2% real but earned -2% real - a 4 pp loss; unexpected inflation of 4 pp (8% vs. 4% expected) created this redistribution from lender to borrower.

prompt: Inflation that is perfectly stable and correctly anticipated by all parties in the economy will not cause wealth redistribution between lenders and borrowers because

options.label: A
options.text: Lenders and borrowers always agree to split inflation gains and losses equally

options.label: B
options.text: Stable inflation makes it impossible for prices to rise, preventing any redistribution

options.label: C
options.text: Perfectly anticipated inflation reduces inflation to zero automatically

options.label: D
options.text: The central bank prevents all redistribution when inflation is constant

options.label: E
options.text: Anticipated price changes are incorporated into nominal contract terms

explanation: If expected inflation = actual inflation, all contracts correctly price the inflation premium. A lender expecting 3% inflation sets a nominal rate that includes a 3% inflation premium - earning the real return they planned; the borrower pays the agreed real cost; no surprise → no arbitrary redistribution; this is why economists distinguish between expected inflation (which can be planned for) and unexpected inflation (which creates MEA-1.H.1 redistribution).

prompt: A professor explains that unexpected inflation hurts "creditors" and helps "debtors." A student asks: "But aren't savers also creditors?" How should the professor respond?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, but savers are only affected by unexpected inflation if they hold foreign currency

options.label: B
options.text: Yes; depositors lend to banks and hold nominal claims

options.label: C
options.text: No — savers and creditors are completely separate groups with no overlap

options.label: D
options.text: No — savers benefit from inflation because higher prices help banks pay higher interest

options.label: E
options.text: No — savers are not creditors; creditors are only banks

explanation: In economics, "creditor" broadly means any holder of a fixed nominal financial claim - including bank depositors (who lend to the bank), bondholders, and pensioners; when you save at a fixed rate, you are a creditor. Unexpected inflation erodes the real return on all fixed nominal claims, whether they are traditional bank loans, deposits, bonds, or pension entitlements; the MEA-1.H.1 principle applies to all fixed nominal claims, not just formal loan contracts.

prompt: A central bank that consistently creates more inflation than it announces (actual inflation > announced target) will over time tend to

options.label: A
options.text: Transfer real wealth from fixed-nominal creditors to debtors

options.label: B
options.text: Benefit the central bank by increasing its revenue from printing money, with no redistribution

options.label: C
options.text: Cause no redistribution because people eventually anticipate the higher inflation

options.label: D
options.text: Help all households equally by raising nominal incomes

options.label: E
options.text: Help the economy grow by stimulating investment and reducing unemployment permanently

explanation: If a central bank consistently delivers higher-than-announced inflation, expected inflation built into contracts will be systematically below actual inflation. This means contracts are persistently miscalibrated - lenders/creditors are consistently surprised by extra inflation, consistently losing real value; borrowers/debtors consistently gain; the redistribution becomes systematic rather than one-time arbitrary; applies repeatedly if inflation surprises are persistent.

prompt: Which of the following would BEST eliminate or greatly reduce the arbitrary wealth redistribution described in MEA-1.H.1?

options.label: A
options.text: Setting nominal interest rates to zero, eliminating the interest rate channel

options.label: B
options.text: Fully indexing nominal contracts to actual inflation

options.label: C
options.text: Requiring all wages to be fixed in nominal terms for 10-year periods

options.label: D
options.text: Requiring lenders to charge higher nominal interest rates than borrowers want to pay

options.label: E
options.text: Banning all lending activity to prevent creditors from being exposed to inflation risk

explanation: The mechanism of MEA-1.H.1 redistribution requires fixed nominal contracts that cannot adjust when actual inflation differs from expected inflation. Inflation indexing breaks this mechanism: if the nominal interest rate, wage, or rent automatically adjusts to reflect actual inflation, neither party suffers a surprise; treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS), variable-rate mortgages, and COLA-indexed wages all serve this function - they transfer inflation risk to the price level rather than to individual parties.

prompt: In which of the following situations would a lender be HELPED rather than hurt by an inflation surprise?

options.label: A
options.text: When actual inflation exceeds expected inflation, the lender earns more in nominal terms

options.label: B
options.text: When inflation is higher than expected, lenders gain because borrowers pay faster

options.label: C
options.text: When actual inflation equals expected inflation, the lender earns extra return

options.label: D
options.text: A lender can never benefit from any inflation scenario under MEA-1.H.1

options.label: E
options.text: When actual inflation is lower than anticipated

explanation: redistribution is symmetric; when actual inflation < expected inflation, the lender earns more real value than planned: fixed nominal repayments purchase more goods and services because prices rose less than expected. This is the flip side - lenders gain when they are pleasantly surprised by lower-than-expected inflation (or unexpected deflation), while borrowers lose; the direction of the redistribution depends entirely on whether actual inflation was higher or lower than expected.

prompt: A government has $5 trillion in nominal fixed-rate debt outstanding. Creditors (bondholders) lent money expecting 3% annual inflation. If actual inflation is 6% for the next decade, which of the following correctly describes the effect on the government and its creditors?

options.label: A
options.text: Creditors are unaffected because government bonds are risk-free

options.label: B
options.text: The government and creditors split the inflation gain equally

options.label: C
options.text: Creditors gain — higher inflation means government tax revenues rise to pay them more

options.label: D
options.text: Government gains as fixed debt erodes; bondholders lose purchasing power

options.label: E
options.text: Both the government and creditors are harmed by the higher inflation

explanation: With $5 trillion in fixed nominal debt and unexpected inflation adding 3 pp per year for 10 years, the real value of government debt is substantially reduced. Bondholders planned to earn (for example) 5% nominal - 3% expected = 2% real; they earn 5% - 6% = -1% real; the government planned to pay 2% real; it actually pays -1% real - a massive windfall funded by the wealth redistribution from bondholders to the government; at the sovereign level.

prompt: A teacher presents this scenario: "Maria lent $10,000 to John at 5% nominal interest for one year. Both expected 2% inflation. Actual inflation was 2%." Then the teacher asks: "Now suppose actual inflation was 10% instead." Compare John's real gain/loss and Maria's real gain/loss in both scenarios. Use real interest ≈ nominal interest − inflation and approximate surprise redistribution = fixed principal × the inflation surprise; hold principal constant.

options.label: A
options.text: Expected real rate: 3%; actual: −5%; surprise transfer: $800 to Maria

options.label: B
options.text: Expected real rate: 5%; actual: −3%; surprise transfer: $500 to John

options.label: C
options.text: Expected real rate: 5%; actual: 5%; surprise transfer: $0

options.label: D
options.text: Expected real rate: 3%; actual: 5%; surprise transfer: $200 to Maria

options.label: E
options.text: Expected real rate: 3%; actual: −5%; surprise transfer: $800 to John

explanation: Scenario 1: No surprise - real rate = 3% for both as planned; scenario 2: The surprise is 10%-2% = 8 pp extra inflation; maria's real return = 5%-10% = -5%; she planned +3%. Maria lost (3%-(-5%)) = 8 pp; john's real cost = -5%; he planned -3%; john gained 8 pp; on $10,000: redistribution = 8% × $10,000 = $800 transferred from Maria to John via the unexpected 8 pp inflation surprise; this is the quintessential MEA-1.H.1 example.

prompt: Why do economists specifically focus on UNEXPECTED inflation rather than ALL inflation when analyzing wealth redistribution between lenders and borrowers?

options.label: A
options.text: Expected price changes can be incorporated into nominal agreements

options.label: B
options.text: Because expected inflation only affects borrowers while unexpected inflation affects everyone

options.label: C
options.text: Because economists do not know how to measure expected inflation

options.label: D
options.text: Because expected inflation is illegal in most countries

options.label: E
options.text: Because only unexpected inflation changes nominal interest rates

explanation: The distinction between expected and unexpected is fundamental to MEA-1.H; expected inflation: lenders build it into nominal rates → they earn their planned real return → no redistribution. Unexpected inflation: by definition, the contract was written before the surprise was known → the nominal rate does not include the extra inflation premium → the lender cannot protect themselves → real value is transferred to the borrower; the harm is specifically a consequence of the inability to plan for what was not anticipated.

prompt: A student argues that unexpected inflation is actually good for the economy because "borrowers gain, and borrowers spend more, which stimulates output." Evaluate this argument.

options.label: A
options.text: Redistribution need not create aggregate gains and can disrupt lending

options.label: B
options.text: The student is correct — the spending multiplier ensures that borrower gains create more output than lender losses

options.label: C
options.text: The student is correct, but only for unexpected deflation, not unexpected inflation

options.label: D
options.text: The student is completely wrong — inflation never stimulates spending

options.label: E
options.text: The student is correct — unexpected inflation always stimulates the economy and should be encouraged

explanation: The student's argument confuses redistribution with net stimulus; when borrowers gain $X from unexpected inflation, lenders lose $X - the total real spending power in the economy is unchanged. Furthermore, if lenders reduce future lending due to the inflation risk premium they now require, real interest rates rise and investment falls - a negative output effect; arbitrary redistribution also creates social inefficiency: resources are transferred based on luck of contract position rather than productive activity.

prompt: A country experiences severe unexpected deflation for two years. Which of the following economic consequences is most directly predicted by MEA-1.H.1?

options.label: A
options.text: Fixed nominal debt becomes more burdensome as prices fall

options.label: B
options.text: Creditors will reduce their real wealth because of the deflation

options.label: C
options.text: Lenders will immediately reduce their lending activity in response to the deflation

options.label: D
options.text: Both lenders and borrowers experience equal harm during deflation

options.label: E
options.text: Borrowers will benefit because falling prices make goods cheaper to purchase

explanation: Unexpected deflation is economically dangerous precisely because of MEA-1.H.1 in reverse; when prices fall unexpectedly, the real burden of fixed nominal debts rises sharply. A farmer who agreed to repay $100 at 5% nominal interest expected prices to be stable or rising - now faces the same nominal repayment but with fewer dollars earned per unit of output sold; debt deflation can trigger a self-reinforcing spiral: higher real debt burdens → defaults → bank failures → credit contraction → more deflation.

options.label: A

Gains ~3 pp of real value vs. plan (the debt is cheaper in real terms than planned); person C: no fixed nominal contracts - not directly subject to the MEA-1.H.1 redistribution mechanism, though faces general price-level effects; the redistribution is specifically between holders of fixed nominal assets (A loses) and fixed nominal liabilities (B gains).

prompt: An economist explains that inflation indexing of contracts can eliminate the redistributive effects of unexpected inflation. Which of the following examples would NOT eliminate redistribution from unexpected inflation?

prompt: A professor presents this problem: "In Country A, lenders and borrowers perfectly forecast inflation every year. In Country B, the inflation rate is volatile and unpredictable, but on average equals Country A's inflation rate over 10 years." Which country has more wealth redistribution between lenders and borrowers from unexpected inflation?

options.label: A
options.text: Both countries have zero redistribution because only the aggregate level matters

options.label: B
options.text: Country A has more redistribution because predictable inflation encourages more contracts

options.label: C

options.label: D

options.label: E
options.text: B's unexpected fluctuations cause more arbitrary transfers than A's predictable inflation

explanation: The key insight: it is not the LEVEL of inflation that causes MEA-1.H.1 redistribution but the SURPRISE (the gap between actual and expected); country A: actual always = expected → zero redistribution despite nonzero inflation. Country B: volatile, unpredictable inflation → frequent large surprises → frequent large redistributions between lenders and borrowers; two countries with the same average inflation rate can have vastly different redistribution experiences based on inflation predictability.

prompt: A pension fund holds $500 million in fixed-rate bonds. Expected inflation when the bonds were purchased was 2.5%. Actual inflation is 5% per year for 10 years. Describe the impact on the pension fund and its beneficiaries.

options.label: A
options.text: Both the pension fund and bond issuers gain equally from higher inflation

options.label: B
options.text: The fund benefits — higher inflation increases stock market returns, protecting pension values

options.label: C
options.text: Fixed bond payments lose more purchasing power than the fund anticipated

options.label: D
options.text: Bond issuers (borrowers) are harmed; the pension fund (lender) benefits

options.label: E
options.text: The fund is unaffected — institutional investors are insulated from inflation surprises

explanation: A pension fund holding fixed-rate bonds is a large-scale lender/creditor; every percentage point of unexpected inflation (above the 2.5% expected) reduces the real return on the bond portfolio. Over 10 years, a 2.5 pp annual real loss compounded is substantial: (1+real return actual)^10 vs; (1+real return expected)^10; retirees relying on these fixed payouts are the ultimate losers; applies at institutional scale: unexpected inflation harms creditors regardless of size.

prompt: A student loan borrower owes $50,000 at a fixed 6% nominal interest rate. She expected 3% inflation when she took the loan (expected real rate = 3%). Actual inflation turns out to be 6% in the first year. What is her approximate real borrowing cost in Year 1, and how does it compare to what she planned?

options.label: A
options.text: Real cost = 3% (her expected rate), unaffected by actual inflation

options.label: B
options.text: Approximately 0% real cost, rather than the expected 3%

options.label: C
options.text: Real cost = 9% (6% + 3%). She paid more than planned

options.label: D
options.text: Real cost = 6% nominal, unchanged from the contract rate

options.label: E

The unexpected 3 pp of extra inflation reduced her real borrowing cost from 3% to 0% - she borrowed at zero real interest rate due to the inflation surprise; the lender's real return fell from 3% to 0%; on $50,000, this redistribution is approximately 3% × $50,000 = $1,500 transferred from lender to borrower in the first year alone.

prompt: Which group among the following is MOST harmed by unexpected DEFLATION (not inflation)?

options.label: E
options.text: Lenders who extended fixed-rate loans before the deflation

explanation: Unexpected deflation reverses the MEA-1.H.1 redistribution: borrowers lose, lenders gain. A firm or household with large fixed-rate debt finds the real burden rises as prices fall - the same nominal repayment represents more real purchasing power; during severe unexpected deflation, heavily indebted borrowers may face insolvency as real debt burdens exceed their real income; this is why debt-deflation spirals can be economically devastating.

prompt: Country X has persistent unexpected inflation of 5 pp above expected inflation for five years (actual is always 5 pp more than expected). Country Y has zero unexpected inflation over five years. If each country starts with the same total wealth distributed equally between lenders and borrowers, after five years

options.label: A
options.text: Country X will have higher total wealth because inflation creates new value

options.label: B
options.text: Both countries will have equal redistribution because the same total wealth exists

options.label: C
options.text: X experiences creditor-to-debtor transfers; Y has no inflation surprise

options.label: D
options.text: Country X and Country Y will have the same distribution of wealth

options.label: E
options.text: Country Y will have more redistribution because lower inflation concentrates wealth

Tenant (fixed rent): 5 pp × ($1,200×12) = 5% × $14,400 = -$720 real gain for tenant; landlord loses -$720; applies simultaneously to all four fixed nominal contracts - each generates a surprise redistribution in the same direction: holders of fixed nominal claims lose; counterparties gain.

prompt: Analyze the following paradox: "When unexpected inflation occurs, the total real wealth in the economy is conserved — the gains to borrowers exactly equal the losses to lenders. So unexpected inflation causes no NET social harm." Is this argument valid? What are economists' counterarguments?

options.label: A
options.text: The argument is fully valid — redistribution is always welfare-neutral

options.label: B
options.text: The argument is valid for moderate inflation but invalid for hyperinflation only

options.label: C
options.text: Unplanned transfers can create real social costs even when claims offset

options.label: D
options.text: The argument is valid — only distributional effects matter, not efficiency effects

options.label: E

explanation: While lender losses ≈ borrower gains in accounting terms, this misses multiple sources of genuine social cost; (1) Arbitrary redistribution: neither party chose or planned for this outcome - contracts are violated in real terms. (2) Inflation risk premiums: future lenders demand higher nominal rates to compensate for uncertainty → higher real borrowing costs → less investment; (3) Credit market contraction: lenders may exit fixed-rate markets. (4) Fixed-income earner harm: retirees, pensioners, workers on fixed wages suffer real hardship that borrower gains do not offset from a welfare perspective; (5) Behavioral distortions: people avoid fixed contracts, making financial planning harder; identifies redistribution as the mechanism - but the full social cost is larger than the zero-sum accounting implies.

prompt: A central bank allowed unexpected inflation of 5 pp above target for three consecutive years, then controlled it. After the three years, a journalist argues: "The inflation is over — the wealth redistribution is done." An economist responds: "No, the redistribution continues through legacy contracts." Explain the economist's point.

options.text: A permanently higher price level leaves existing nominal claims worth less

options.label: B
options.text: The journalist is correct — redistribution stops immediately when inflation stops

options.label: C
options.text: The redistribution stops when inflation stops because nominal values reset

options.label: D
options.text: The economist is making an error — only current-period inflation matters

options.label: E
options.text: The economist is correct only if the central bank raises rates after the inflation period

explanation: redistribution is locked in at the moment of the unexpected inflation surprise, for the remaining life of the affected contracts. If a 30-year bond was issued during the unexpected inflation at a nominal rate that now implies a negative real return (because inflation was 5 pp higher than priced in), that negative real return persists for the bond's remaining life regardless of subsequent inflation. The redistribution (from bondholder to issuer) is crystallized for the duration of the contract; only when the contract matures and new contracts are written at the new (correctly anticipated) nominal rate does the redistribution fully end for that contract.

Making product prices and labor market wages more flexible (shorter-duration adjustments) would reduce the duration of the surprise and limit redistribution for those markets. However, it does not solve the problem for long-term financial contracts (30-year mortgages, 10-year bonds) which by their nature fix terms at origination; contract indexation directly targets the mechanism; price flexibility addresses a different market rigidity; the proposal partially addresses some redistribution but misses the financial-contract dimension.

prompt: An economist makes a provocative argument: "Moderate expected inflation of 2-3% is actually beneficial because it ensures borrowers always benefit slightly, stimulating investment and economic activity." Use MEA-1.H.1 to critique this argument.

options.label: A
options.text: The argument correctly identifies that expected inflation stimulates investment through lower real interest rates

options.label: B
options.text: The argument is correct — moderate expected inflation is always beneficial for all parties

options.label: C
options.text: The argument is correct — expected inflation always helps borrowers borrow more

options.label: D
options.text: The argument is correct only for countries with high debt-to-GDP ratios

options.label: E
options.text: Expected inflation can enter contracts; only surprises create unplanned redistribution

explanation: Key error in the economist's argument: expected inflation does not redistribute wealth - it is fully priced into nominal rates; lenders set nominal rates = real rate + EXPECTED inflation. If inflation is 2% and expected, nominal rate = real rate + 2%; the borrower pays the real rate - no windfall; the MEA-1.H.1 gain to borrowers requires actual inflation > expected inflation (the surprise). There is no systematic "borrower benefit" from expected inflation in terms of wealth redistribution; any claim that expected inflation stimulates investment through lower ex post real rates confuses ex ante and ex post and misunderstands how nominal rates are set.

prompt: Compose the most comprehensive summary of all parties HARMED and all parties BENEFITED by unexpected inflation, using MEA-1.H.1 as the framework. Then explain the single unifying principle that distinguishes gainers from losers.

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Only lenders and only borrowers are affected; no other parties are relevant

options.label: C

options.label: D

explanation: The unifying principle: FIXED NOMINAL ASSET → loses real value when unexpected inflation occurs; FIXED NOMINAL LIABILITY → gains real value when unexpected inflation occurs. This captures every party: lenders hold fixed nominal assets (loans owed to them) → lose; borrowers hold fixed nominal liabilities (loans owed by them) → gain. Fixed-rate savers, bondholders, pensioners, fixed-wage workers, fixed-rent landlords, fixed-price sellers are all on the fixed-nominal-asset side; borrowers, fixed-rate mortgage holders, bond issuers, employers paying fixed wages, tenants, fixed-price buyers are on the fixed-nominal-liability side; is a single principle applied across all fixed nominal contract positions in the economy.

Industrialists: held fixed nominal debts that were also destroyed in real terms - they could repay billions of marks worth essentially nothing; the redistribution was catastrophic and historically unprecedented. The same mechanism as MEA-1.H.1 applies: unexpected inflation transferred real wealth from fixed nominal asset holders to fixed nominal liability holders - at hyperinflation scale, this meant the complete destruction of the savings class and the enrichment of the debtor class.

Using MEA-1.H.1, evaluate how each component addresses the unexpected-inflation redistribution problem and predict the combined effect on wealth redistribution between lenders/creditors and borrowers/debtors.

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Credible targets reduce surprises; indexed wages and bonds protect contracted values

options.label: C

options.label: D

explanation: This synthesis question tests the full application of MEA-1.H.1; component 1 attacks the root cause: if no surprise occurs (actual = expected), MEA-1.H.1 redistribution is zero for ALL contracts.
